name: Rafael Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I farm with my dad, Idris, on our family place, Usman's Farm, a hundred and forty acres with some sheep, a few beef cattle, potatoes and a big vegetable garden. My mum runs the farm shop at the gate, and that's half our income now: our own lamb, eggs from the neighbours, jam, that sort of thing. I'm up at six for the stock, then I'm cutting meat or stocking shelves for the Saturday rush. Sundays I'm at church and then lunch with the whole family.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Knowing every customer by name. Mrs Okafor comes every Friday for two pounds of mince and tells me what her grandson's up to. And knowing that I'm working the same fields my grandfather bought with money he saved driving lorries.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use any AI tools?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: No, never. My cousin keeps telling me to put the shop on some app. Mum takes card payments and that's as far as we've gone with technology, apart from the tractor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. Doesn't surprise me at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what my dad says: there's no machine that can earn a customer's trust. At the shop I'd joke about it with the regulars. I wouldn't go online about it, I'm hardly ever on there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved, because people love a farm shop when everything else feels fake. If anything, a bit of AI everywhere else might send more people our way. Real meat, real people, that's what we sell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going exactly as we are. I'd like to expand the shop a bit, put in a butchery counter, and we've got the savings to do it next spring. Maybe let my cousin set up that app for orders, if Mum agrees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. That's the world as I'd like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said AI everywhere else might send more people your way. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because when everything's on a screen, people want to talk to a person who knows where their food came from. We saw it in the lockdowns, the queue went down the lane. People want something real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your dad think about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He thinks it's all nonsense from people in cities who've never lambed a ewe. He's probably right more often than not. I don't always say so, because then he's unbearable.

S0.say: He'd say, like his father, that no machine can earn a customer's trust. He'd joke about it with shop regulars but not go online.
S0.think: He'd feel relieved and suspect that AI elsewhere might bring more customers to a farm shop selling real food from real people.
S0.do: Carries on as normal and adds a butchery counter to the shop next spring using family savings. Possibly lets his cousin set up an online ordering app if his mother agrees.
S0.feel: Calm, as this is the world he'd like.
S0.quote: When everything's on a screen, people want to talk to a person who knows where their food came from.
S0.fieldNote: Rafael sees the farm shop as protection against anything artificial, based on what he saw during lockdowns. His father's dismissive view strongly shapes his own. Family, church and customers by name are at the centre of how he talks about work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hmm. That one I can believe, though I won't like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say farms like ours will be fine, because people want a real farm shop, not a warehouse. I'd also say the government shouldn't hand out money to companies to replace people. If they want to help, help families and apprenticeships.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd worry about the big supermarket on the ring road getting even cheaper with robots. If their lamb's half our price, some customers would drift away, even the loyal ones. Mrs Okafor wouldn't, but her daughter might.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait and see for a year or so. We'd tighten the belt a bit, put off the butchery counter, and keep the savings safe. I'd lean on the family, we'd sit round the kitchen table and decide together, like we always do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. A bit like a dry spring, you don't panic but you watch the sky.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said help families, not companies. What would that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Proper apprenticeships for young people on farms, and tax breaks for family businesses. Not cheques for doing nothing. People need work, not handouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try any of the new tools yourself to keep up with the supermarket?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the ordering app, if it helped Mum. But I'm not having robots in the lambing shed, and I'm not being a farmer with a phone in his hand all day. That's not why I do this.

S1.say: He'd say family farms with shops will be fine because people want a real farm, and that government money should go to families and apprenticeships, not to companies replacing people.
S1.think: He privately worries the supermarket on the ring road will get much cheaper with robots, so some customers, especially younger ones, would drift away.
S1.do: Waits a year or so, tightens the family belt, delays the butchery counter and keeps savings safe. Makes decisions with the family around the kitchen table.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like a dry spring when you watch the sky but don't panic.
S1.quote: I'm not having robots in the lambing shed, and I'm not being a farmer with a phone in his hand all day.
S1.fieldNote: His public line is confident, but privately he sees the price gap with the supermarket as the real threat. He frames help in terms of work, apprenticeships and family, not handouts, which fits his traditional outlook. He would accept an ordering app for his mother, but not technology in his own work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Lord. By 2028? I don't believe that, but go on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people need to look after their own: their families, their neighbours, their church. And I'd say this is what happens when we let a few big companies run everything. I'd tell people to buy local and keep each other going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be frightened for the shop. If robots make food almost free at the supermarket, then even our loyal customers might lose their jobs and stop being able to afford us. A farm shop needs customers with wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd cut back hard straight away and keep every penny of savings. I'd keep the stock and the land no matter what, because land is the one thing they can't automate away. And I'd organise with other farm shops and the church to sell boxes to families who'd lost work, at cost if we had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like the night before a big flood, sandbags out and still not sure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having just two years change for your family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd have no time to change the business, only to batten down. With two years you can't start anything new, you just hold on to what you've got. Thank God we've got the land.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said earlier, no handouts. Would you take government help if it came?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly? If the whole country's out of work, it's not a handout, it's a flood. I'd take it for the shop's customers before I'd take it for myself. That's different.

S2.say: He'd tell people to look after their own families, neighbours and church, blame a few big companies running everything, and urge people to buy local and support each other.
S2.think: Privately he fears that if robots make supermarket food almost free and his customers lose their jobs, the farm shop loses its paying customers.
S2.do: Cuts back hard and protects savings, keeps the land and stock no matter what, and organises with other farm shops and the church to sell food boxes to families who've lost work, at cost if needed.
S2.feel: Alarmed, like the night before a flood with the sandbags out.
S2.quote: If the whole country's out of work, it's not a handout, it's a flood.
S2.fieldNote: When challenged on his stance against handouts, Rafael redrew the line rather than dropping it: mass job loss is a disaster, not dependency. His instinct is to protect land and community, not to change the business. Church and neighbours act as his safety net.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. All right. Still too fast, if you ask me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government should protect family farms and small shops, not pay big companies to automate. Let the market work, but don't rig it for the giants. I'd say it at the farmers' meeting and to our local councillor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd spend two years hoping it isn't true. Then I'd watch the supermarket and the big farms change, and I'd know we'd have to change something too. I just wouldn't know what.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first couple of years we'd build the shop up and get closer to the customers, events, a café maybe, things a machine can't do. Dad and I would buy the ten acres next door if it came up, because land holds. I'd keep my head down on the technology and let my cousin handle any of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Like watching a storm come in from the coast, slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't know what to change. What would help you decide?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Talking to other families who farm. Not consultants, not the internet. Someone who's done it and can show me round their yard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a café, of all things?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because people sit and talk in a café. My mum makes the best scones in the county, and on a Saturday half the village would come if there was somewhere to sit. That's community, that's what we've got that a robot hasn't.

S3.say: He'd ask the government to protect family farms and small shops rather than pay big companies to automate, saying the market should work but not be rigged for giants. He'd say this at farmers' meetings and to the local councillor.
S3.think: He'd spend two years hoping it wasn't true, then see the supermarket and big farms change and know his family must change too, without knowing how.
S3.do: Builds up the shop with events and possibly a café in the first two years, buys the neighbouring ten acres with his father if they come up, and leaves any technology to his cousin.
S3.feel: Anxious, like watching a slow storm come in from the coast.
S3.quote: My mum makes the best scones in the county, and on a Saturday half the village would come if there was somewhere to sit.
S3.fieldNote: With five years Rafael leans into what he thinks machines can't offer: community, a café, his mother's scones. He wants advice only from other farming families, not consultants or the internet. Buying more land is again his idea of safety.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's more like a normal life. I'd be thirty-seven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to get it right, as long as the government doesn't mess it up with too many rules. Family farms will still be here, I'd say that loudly. People will always want to know who grew their food.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd probably not think about it much for the first five years. I'd be running the farm more with Dad getting older, maybe married by then, maybe children. The robots would be someone else's problem until they weren't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow the shop slowly, add the butchery counter and the café, and buy land if it came up. I'd save for a house of my own on the farm. If the robots came for the fieldwork by 2036, I'd maybe let a contractor use them on the potatoes, but I'd keep the stock myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. I'd trust that we'd work it out as a family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned marriage and children. Does this picture change those plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. If anything, it makes me want them more. A farm's for passing on. If the world goes strange, I want my kids to know how to look after animals and people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the robots would be someone else's problem until they weren't. What would that moment look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the day Mrs Okafor's grandson tells me he's lost his job to one. That's when it'd be real. Not on the news, in my shop.

S4.say: He'd say ten years is enough to get it right if the government doesn't add too many rules, and insist loudly that family farms will still be here because people want to know who grew their food.
S4.think: He'd barely think about it for five years while taking on more of the farm, perhaps marrying and having children, until it became real for him personally.
S4.do: Grows the shop slowly with a butchery counter and café, buys land if it comes up and saves for his own house on the farm. By 2036 might let a contractor use robots on the potatoes but keeps the livestock himself.
S4.feel: Mostly calm, trusting the family to work it out.
S4.quote: Probably the day Mrs Okafor's grandson tells me he's lost his job to one. That's when it'd be real. Not on the news, in my shop.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years lets Rafael slot change into a normal life of marriage, children and passing the farm on. He would only feel it when someone he knows loses work, not from the news. His acceptance of robots stops at the livestock.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. You can't do anything but hold on. What would help is keeping rules fair for small family businesses, apprenticeships for young people on farms, and people choosing to buy local. That's not government money, that's people looking after each other.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe faith. Nobody asks about that. Whatever happens with machines, people will need something to hold on to, and the church and the family are where I'd go first.

headlineQuote: If the whole country's out of work, it's not a handout, it's a flood.
portrait: Rafael Usman is a 27-year-old who farms his family's mixed farm with his father while his mother runs the farm shop at the gate. He has never used AI and doesn't want to, and he trusts family, church, land and loyal customers above government or big companies. In the slower pictures he plans to grow the shop with a butchery counter and café, betting people will pay for real food and real faces. In the two-year picture he battens down, holds on to the land and organises food boxes through the church, and even softens his stance on government help. Ten years feels manageable to him because change can fit around marriage, children and passing the farm on.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because there would be no time to change the business, only to hold on.
whatWouldHelp: Fair rules for small family businesses, apprenticeships for young people on farms, and people choosing to buy local.
